KafkaPublish, Publish in the prelude, is the plain publish policy; every publish waits for the cluster's delivery report. A mount site names it wherever a registration publishes: .out_reply(Publish::default()) for a reply, .out(Slot, Publish::default()) for a slot, .out_retry(Publish::default()) for retry copies. The policy holds no connection; the runtime pairs it with the connected broker at startup into a KafkaPublisher. A registration that names no policy for its reply publishes through this one. A publish returns once the cluster has acknowledged the record, as the producer's durability settings define it, or with the error it reported. librdkafka queues records locally and sends them in batches; a full queue makes a publish wait for room, which slows the handler to the pace of the cluster. queue_timeout bounds that wait: past it the publish fails with a queue-full error. A reply goes to one topic and does not wait for an answer from the reader. A synchronous exchange is a reply topic of the service's own plus a correlation header the requester sets and the responder copies to its reply. Per record, a publish carries a key or a partition; RoundRobin spreads replies over the partitions.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_publishing_publish.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]), |b| { // A full local queue fails the reply after five seconds instead of holding the // handler until librdkafka has room again. b.include(confirm) .out_reply(Publish::default().queue_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5))); }, ) } examples/manual/kafka_publishing_publish.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]), |b| { let confirm = subscriber("orders", Confirm).map_source(|_| orders()); // A full local queue fails the reply after five seconds instead of holding the // handler until librdkafka has room again. b.include(confirm.reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default().queue_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5))); }, ) }

Durability is the producer's acks; an idempotent producer with Commit::Tracked gives at-least-once from input to output. producer_config sets a librdkafka producer property on the broker, for every publisher of the service. acks says which replicas confirm a record before a publish returns: all waits for every in-sync replica. enable.idempotence makes the producer number its sends, so the cluster writes a record once even when the producer sends it again. librdkafka checks the values when the broker connects, so a wrong value stops the service at startup. A handler that replies settles its input after the reply's publish returned. Under Commit::Tracked the input's offset is committed only then, so a crash before it brings the input back and the reply is sent again. A reader of the output can therefore see a reply twice; exactly once takes a transactional pipeline.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_publishing_durability.rs /// The input's offset is committed once the receipt is acknowledged by every in-sync replica, /// so a crash in between brings the payment back instead of losing the receipt. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("payments").group("receipts-svc").commit(Commit::Tracked), reply)] async fn issue_receipt(payment: &Payment) -> Receipt { Receipt { payment_id: payment.id, } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // Every in-sync replica confirms a record, and a retried send is written once. let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]) .producer_config("acks", "all") .producer_config("enable.idempotence", "true"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("receipts", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(issue_receipt).out_reply(Publish::default()); }) } examples/manual/kafka_publishing_durability.rs /// The input's offset is committed once the receipt is acknowledged by every in-sync replica, /// so a crash in between brings the payment back instead of losing the receipt. struct IssueReceipt; impl Handle<Payment, Receipt> for IssueReceipt { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Receipt { payment_id: payment.id, })) } } fn payments() -> KafkaTopic { KafkaTopic::new("payments") .group("receipts-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) } fn app() -> impl App { // Every in-sync replica confirms a record, and a retried send is written once. let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]) .producer_config("acks", "all") .producer_config("enable.idempotence", "true"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("receipts", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let issue = subscriber("payments", IssueReceipt).map_source(|_| payments()); b.include(issue.reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default()); }) }

The partition-key header, PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, becomes the record's native key, so records sharing a key land on one partition, in order. The header is named kafka-partition-key. On publish its value becomes the Kafka record key and does not travel as a header of its own. Kafka's partitioner hashes the key, so every record of one key goes to one partition, and a consumer reads them in the order they were written. A message type declares the header in its typed header contract, #[outgoing(headers = ..)], with a field renamed to kafka-partition-key; a HeaderMap with that entry works the same. On consume the header holds the record key again, and a handler reads the key as raw bytes through the Key context key. workers(n, by_key) with LaneKey::RecordKey keeps the same order inside one consumer: records of one key run on one lane. A partition step places a record ahead of its key.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_publishing_keys.rs /// The header a shipment carries: `kafka-partition-key`, which becomes the record key. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize)] struct ShipmentKey { #[serde(rename = "kafka-partition-key")] customer: String, } /// Every shipment of one customer lands on one partition, so its consumer sees them in order. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shipments", headers = ShipmentKey)] struct Shipment { order_id: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Shipment)] struct Shipments; #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("orders").group("shipping"))] async fn ship(order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl Publisher, Shipments>) -> HandlerOutcome { let key = ShipmentKey { customer: order.customer.clone(), }; let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; if shipments .message(&shipment) .with_headers(&key) .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_publishing_keys.rs /// The header a shipment carries: `kafka-partition-key`, which becomes the record key. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct ShipmentKey { #[serde(rename = "kafka-partition-key")] customer: String, } /// Every shipment of one customer lands on one partition, so its consumer sees them in order. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "shipments", headers = ShipmentKey)] struct Shipment { order_id: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Shipment)] struct Shipments; struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let key = ShipmentKey { customer: order.customer.clone(), }; let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; outs.get(Shipments) .message(&shipment) .with_headers(&key) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } fn orders() -> KafkaTopic { KafkaTopic::new("orders").group("shipping") }

The partition step pins one record to a partition, ahead of its key and the partitioner. It is a per-record setting of Kafka's publisher, KafkaOptions, written by a step of the publish builder. A handler reaches the step through a slot bounded on those options: Out<impl Publisher<Options = KafkaOptions>, Slot>, with this crate's prelude imported. The bound keeps the step off a publisher of another broker. The record goes to exactly that partition; its key still travels with it. A partition the topic does not have fails the publish, and the handler decides what follows. A test reads the setting back from the slot with tb.out::<Slot>().with_options(..). The in-process cluster gives every topic one partition, so a pin to partition 0 lands and a pin to any other is refused, as a cluster refuses a partition its topic lacks.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_publishing_partition.rs /// Each partition of `dispatch.lanes` is one courier lane, read by that lane's courier alone, so /// a pickup goes to the partition its order names. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("dispatch.orders").group("dispatch"))] async fn dispatch( order: &Order, Out(lanes): Out<impl Publisher<Options = KafkaOptions>, Lanes>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let pickup = Pickup { order_id: order.id }; if let Err(err) = lanes.message(&pickup).partition(order.lane).publish().await { tracing::warn!(order.id, order.lane, %err, "pickup not dispatched"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_publishing_partition.rs /// Each partition of `dispatch.lanes` is one courier lane, read by that lane's courier alone, so /// a pickup goes to the partition its order names. struct Dispatch; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Dispatch where Entry: OutEntry<Lanes, Wire: Publisher<Options = KafkaOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let pickup = Pickup { order_id: order.id }; let sent = outs .get(Lanes) .message(&pickup) .partition(order.lane) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { tracing::warn!(order.id, order.lane, %err, "pickup not dispatched"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } fn orders() -> KafkaTopic { KafkaTopic::new("dispatch.orders").group("dispatch") }

RoundRobin spreads replies over a fixed partition count, placing only records with no key and no partition. librdkafka places a keyless record by its partitioner, which may keep a whole batch on one partition. When every message takes about the same long time to process, that leaves one consumer busy and its peers idle. RoundRobin::partitions(n) pins each record to the next partition of the cycle 0, 1, ..., n - 1, one record each. It is a transform of the publish position, written after the policy: .out_reply(Publish::default()).transform(RoundRobin::partitions(n)). It writes the same setting as the partition step, so it mounts over Kafka's publisher only. A record that carries a key or already names a partition keeps its placement. The count is fixed at the mount site and matches the destination topic: a smaller one leaves the last partitions empty, a larger one makes publishes fail.

A reply that already names a partition or carries a record key keeps // its placement. The count matches the partitions of `planner.work-items`. b.include(plan) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .transform(RoundRobin::partitions(8)); }) } examples/manual/kafka_distribution.rs /// The service on the cluster `broker` connects to. fn service(broker: KafkaBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("planner", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let plan = subscriber("planner.orders", Plan).map_source(|_| orders()); // Every reply targets the next partition of the cycle (0, 1, ..., 7, 0, ...), one // record each. SchemaRegistry is the Confluent Schema Registry client: it sends nothing until the first lookup, and its clones share one cache. SchemaRegistry::new records the base URL, so the app starts with no registry reachable. basic_auth and bearer_token set the credentials of every request, and HTTPS goes through rustls. request_timeout bounds each request, ten seconds by default, so a registry that accepts the connection and goes silent fails the lookup with KafkaError::SchemaRegistryTimeout. The client is configured before it is handed out, because clones keep the settings they were made from. Every clone reads and writes one cache, so a schema or a subject is fetched once per process. schema_by_id answers from the cache or asks the registry once; cached_schema and cached_subject read the cache alone. A RegisteredSchema carries the id, the SchemaType (Avro, Protobuf or JSON) and the definition text. A registry-backed payload carries the Confluent envelope: a zero byte, the schema id, then the datum. A broker meets it in one of two ways. The codecs, AvroCodec and SchemaFramed, hold the format where a serializer belongs and take their schemas through a SchemaPrefetch. The transcode converts at the broker's edges and leaves the handlers on plain JSON. The example holds the client as application state, and a handler asks it which schema a record was written with.

SchemaCachePolicy bounds the id entries and ages the subject entries, since an id never changes and a subject's latest version moves. The registry assigns an id per distinct schema, so an entry keyed by id is never stale; it takes a bound and no expiry. A subject's latest version moves whenever someone registers one, so its entry takes an expiry and no bound. Cached holds up to capacity ids, drops the oldest past it, and trusts a subject's version for subject_ttl. The default keeps 1000 ids and never looks a subject up again, as Confluent's own clients do. Disabled remembers nothing: the transcode works under it, and the synchronous codecs, which read the cache and cannot await a miss, do not. subject_ttl governs the async lookups: warm and the publish side of the transcode. A codec resolves its subject once, at connect, and keeps it. Ids are numbered per schema context, so one client stays inside one context; an app that reaches across contexts uses a client per context. SchemaRegistry::cache_policy sets the policy of the default cache, MemorySchemaCache. with_cache puts a SchemaCache of your own in its place. That trait is synchronous, because a codec reads it while it encodes or decodes; fetching belongs to the RegistryClient.

parse_envelope and encode_envelope read and write the Confluent wire format: a zero byte, the schema id, the datum. The schema id takes four bytes, big-endian. parse_envelope splits a payload into the id and a view of the datum, with no copy. It returns None for a payload that does not open with the zero byte or is shorter than five bytes, which reads as "not framed". encode_envelope writes the five bytes and the datum into a new buffer. Neither function reaches a registry. A handler that works on the framed bytes takes them through the byte lanes: a #[derive(Deserialized)] view of the delivery in, a #[derive(Serialized)] buffer out. No codec runs on either side, so the bytes travel as they are. The example moves records between two registries and rewrites the id each record names.

schema_registry on the broker and the SchemaFrame layer convert framed payloads to and from plain JSON at the broker's edges. The handler and its models stay on the default JSON codec and never see the envelope. On the way in, every subscription of the broker reads the envelope of a framed delivery, resolves the schema its id names and hands the handler a plain JSON document. A payload with no envelope passes through untouched. A lookup that fails leaves the delivery as it arrived, with a warning, and the handler's decode settles it. On the way out, the layer, added once with RustStream::publish_layer, resolves the subject of each publish's destination topic and frames the payload in that subject's format: a JSON subject keeps the document under the envelope, and an Avro or Protobuf subject is converted to its own format. The subject is {topic}-value unless SubjectStrategy or a pin names another. The layer resolves a subject on its first publish to the topic and remembers the answer. A topic whose subject the registry does not hold publishes plain JSON, so registry-backed and plain topics share one app. A registry that cannot be reached, or a payload that does not fit the schema, fails the publish, and the publishing handler asks for a redelivery. The registry comes to the app as one SchemaRegistry value; the broker and the layer share it, and with it one cache. A producer owns its subjects, so the example registers the reply's subject at startup with register_json. The transcode takes a hop through JSON per message. The codecs (SchemaFramed, AvroCodec) are the other path, and a broker uses one of the two.

MissingSubject decides what a codec does when the registry no longer holds its subject: refuse, register the type's schema, or publish unframed. The policy is set on the prefetch with on_missing_subject before codecs are built from it, and it runs when the broker connects. Refuse, the default, stops the app with an error that names the subject: a registry is a shared contract, and creating a subject in it belongs to whoever owns the topic. AutoRegister registers the schema the type carries under the subject and logs a warning; it suits a producer that owns its subjects. PublishUnframed writes the bare datum and logs a warning, for a topic that must outlive its registry; a registry-backed consumer cannot read those records. The two deletions of a subject differ. A soft delete hides the subject while its ids still resolve, so consumers keep reading and only the producer meets the policy. A permanent delete removes the ids too, and a record that names one of them no longer decodes anywhere. Registering the schema again afterwards mints a new id. The transcode reads a missing subject as a plain topic and publishes JSON there. Naming a codec declares its topic registry-backed, so the policy belongs to the codecs.

register, register_json and register_avro put a schema under a subject; warm resolves an existing subject and registers nothing. Registering is an explicit step of the producer that owns the subject, usually in on_startup. The registry keeps the id of a schema it already holds, so registering the same schema again changes nothing. A schema that the subject's compatibility level refuses fails the call, and the error carries the registry's account of what differs. Each call caches the subject, so the SchemaFrame layer finds it without a request. register_json::<T> registers the JSON Schema that JsonSchema (schemars, re-exported) derives for T. register_avro::<T> registers the Avro schema that AvroSchema derives, in full: field defaults, aliases and docs stay, because a later reader resolves an older writer's datum with them. register takes a SchemaType and the definition text, which is how a Protobuf subject is registered from its .proto source. The registry paths of this crate read Protobuf schemas whose imports come from the well-known types. warm resolves a subject's latest version and caches it, and fails when the registry has no such subject. It is the startup check of a subject that another team owns. lookup_id returns the id a subject already gave one exact schema, and is_compatible asks whether the subject would accept a schema; neither registers anything. A codec registers in its own sense: AvroCodec::register and SchemaFramed::register record the subject a type publishes under, and the SchemaPrefetch resolves those subjects when the broker connects. The registry itself is named twice in such an app, building the prefetch and attaching it, and never at a mount site.

RegistryClient is the transport the registry speaks through; HttpRegistryClient is the default, and with_client supplies another. SchemaRegistry is a facade over two parts: a RegistryClient that asks the registry, and a SchemaCache that remembers the answers. The codecs, the prefetch and the transcode are written against the facade, so a client of your own reaches all of them. It suits a different HTTP stack, a published client crate, a binding to a client in another language, or schemas shipped with the service. A client answers four questions, each as a boxed future: a schema by id, a subject's latest version, registering a schema, and the id of a schema a subject already holds. latest answers None for a subject the registry does not hold, which the transcode reads as a plain topic. is_compatible has a default that answers None, "cannot tell", and the prefetch then skips its compatibility check. The client is shared as Arc<dyn RegistryClient>, so each round trip costs one virtual call and one allocation beside the network, and only a lookup the cache does not answer makes one. basic_auth, bearer_token and request_timeout configure the shipped HTTP client, and a supplied client carries its own credentials and deadlines. Errors are KafkaError::SchemaRegistry, with a message that names what was asked.

SchemaFramed wraps a codec such as JsonCodec in the Confluent envelope, so a registry-backed JSON topic is a codec choice. A JSON document reads without its schema, so the envelope separates from the format: the inner codec writes and reads the document, and SchemaFramed puts the envelope on and takes it off. Decoding strips the envelope and looks nothing up. Encoding frames with the id of the subject that register::<T>(subject) records for T, found by the name serde gives the value's type. The JSON Schema of T is captured with it, for MissingSubject::AutoRegister. The wrapper frames and does not validate: the registry enforces compatibility between versions, and a service that validates each message passes an inner codec that does. SchemaFramed::new takes the SchemaPrefetch that the broker carries, which resolves the registered subjects at connect. The codec named with with_broker_codec decodes the deliveries of its scope, and a reply names it at its own position with .out_reply(policy).codec(codec). An Avro datum cannot be read without its writer schema, so Avro has a codec of its own, AvroCodec.

SchemaPrefetch resolves every registered subject at connect, which keeps the codecs' encode and decode free of I/O. A codec is synchronous, and a registry lookup is not. The prefetch is the async half: every codec built from it, AvroCodec::registry or SchemaFramed::new, records its registered subjects on it. KafkaBroker::schema_prefetch attaches it, and the broker's connect resolves each subject before the app takes a delivery. On the consume path the prefetch resolves the writer schema that an arriving envelope names before the codec decodes the delivery, and leaves the payload as it arrived. A lookup that fails there is logged, and the decode that follows settles the delivery by the subscription's failure policy. The registry appears twice in an app: once building the prefetch, once attaching it. A mount site never names it. Every codec comes from the one prefetch, and what varies per mount is the subject. A Router inside a broker scope overrides the scope's codec for the handlers it carries, by the usual codec cascade. check_compatibility is on by default. At connect each registered type's schema is checked the way registering it would be, against the versions the subject's compatibility level names: the latest one, or every version under a _TRANSITIVE level. A model that has drifted from its subject stops the app, and the error carries the registry's own account of the difference. check_compatibility(false) turns the check off, for a registry whose level is NONE. A subject the registry does not hold is settled by MissingSubject. The prefetch and the transcode are alternatives on one broker: the prefetch reads the envelope, and the transcode replaces it with JSON.

SubjectStrategy names a subject from the topic, the record name or both, and SchemaFrame::subject pins the subject of one topic. The strategies are Confluent's three. TopicName, the default, is {topic}-value: one value schema per topic. RecordName is the record's fully qualified name: one subject per record type, shared by every topic that carries it. TopicRecordName is {topic}-{record}: several record types on one topic, each with its own subject. subject(topic, record) builds the name. The SchemaFrame layer derives a topic's subject with its strategy, TopicName unless subject_strategy names another. The publish path knows the topic and not the record name, so a topic under a record strategy gets its subject pinned with subject(topic, subject), which overrides the strategy for that topic. The example pins the subject that RecordName gives the record. The Protobuf publish policy and its layer take the same three settings.

Another registry stack does the schema work and the byte lanes carry its framed bytes, so no type crosses between the two. A service that already uses a registry crate, such as schema_registry_converter, keeps it. The handler takes the delivery as a #[derive(Deserialized)] view of its bytes and hands them to the converter, which resolves the schema the envelope names through its own client and cache. The reply is the framed buffer the converter returns, in a #[derive(Serialized)] type, and the lane publishes it as it is. No codec runs on either side. Such a crate pins its own apache-avro and prost, and those versions may differ from this crate's. On this path only bytes pass between the two, so the versions never meet. The converter is application state, built in on_startup and read with State. The broker carries neither schema_registry nor schema_prefetch: the schemas are the converter's business. The same shape fits any client that produces bytes, a binding to a client in another language included.

#[derive(Schema)] checks a message type against the newest migration of every subject in schemas/ that declares its record, when the crate compiles. The repository holds the schemas this service owns, one directory per subject, one file per subject version. cargo kafka-schema writes those files and keeps them in step with the registry. The derive comes with the schema-check feature as schema::Schema. The type is bound to its migrations by its record's full name: #[avro(namespace = ..)] plus the type's name, com.acme.orders.Order. The derive finds every subject whose newest migration declares that record and checks the type against each of them. A nested record without a subject of its own is checked through every subject that holds it. A type no migration declares carries no check. For a subject this service owns, the type equals the newest migration. Field names, kinds, nullability (an Option against ["null", T]), nested record names, #[avro(default = ..)] defaults and the whole canonical form are compared. A field with #[avro(with = ..)] or #[serde(flatten)] is checked for its presence only. For an external subject (owner = "external") the type is a reader of every pulled version under Avro's resolution rules: int promotes to long, float or double, string and bytes convert, and a field the writer lacks needs a default. An enum whose variants each wrap one model, the core's #[derive(InMessages)] set, derives Schema too. It maps each variant to its model's record full name, and each model is checked by its own derive. The check is constants, uncalled code and trait bounds. A release binary holds no schema text, and the delivery and publish paths are the same as without it. Schema ids stay resolved at startup by SchemaPrefetch. Switches, read when the crate compiles: RUSTSTREAM_SCHEMA_DIR names another directory than schemas/ beside Cargo.toml. RUSTSTREAM_SCHEMA_REGISTRY=<url> also compares the lock with the registry's version list, once per subject per compiler process: drift fails the build, and a migration not registered yet is a warning. RUSTSTREAM_SCHEMA_OFFLINE=true reads the migrations and the lock only. It is the setting for rust-analyzer (rust-analyzer.cargo.extraEnv). RUSTSTREAM_SCHEMA_EXPORT=<dir> emits no checks: cargo kafka-schema sets it to export a changed type before its migration exists. Recursive Avro records are checked by cargo kafka-schema check only, and a named type referenced twice is compared in its expanded form.

#[derive(Schema)] with #[schema(namespace = ..)] compares the type's serde shape with the JSON Schema of every subject that declares it. The claim is about serde, not about the struct's fields. Every value the type serializes is valid under the subject's schema, and every value the schema admits deserializes into the type. An owned subject is checked in both directions; an external one in the second only, because the service only reads it. A JSON Schema names no record, so the subject's subject.toml records the anchor, record = "com.acme.carts.Cart": the namespace plus the type's name. The derive reads serde's own attributes with serde_derive_internals: rename, rename_all, default, skip, skip_serializing_if, flatten, deny_unknown_fields, transparent and enum tagging mean what serde makes of them. The standard types carry their shape: integers, floats, bool, String, Option, Vec, string maps and serde_json::Value, and with the uuid and chrono features their types. A field of another type contributes that type's shape, so nested types keep their own attributes. What is compared: properties and required: property names equal the serde names; a required property is written on every value, an optional one deserializes when absent. null: the schema admits null exactly when the field is an Option. integer and number: the range from format (int8 .. uint64), narrowed by minimum and maximum; a bare integer reads as signed 64-bit. string and its format (uuid, date-time), and an enum of strings after rename_all. oneOf from an externally, internally or adjacently tagged enum, branch for variant, payloads included. items, additionalProperties against deny_unknown_fields and flattened maps, $ref into $defs or definitions, and $ref to another subject through [[references]] in subject.toml. A construct a Rust type cannot promise (pattern, minLength, multipleOf, not, if, patternProperties, oneOf against an untagged enum, tuples, a recursive $ref) is a compile error that names the keyword and its JSON pointer. #[schema(unchecked)] on the field then checks its presence and optionality only, and cargo kafka-schema check still compares the exported schema with the migration exactly. Drafts 04 to 2020-12 are read.

Cart and Item match the JSON Schema of carts-value. examples/kafka_schema_json.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema, Schema)] #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")] #[schema(namespace = "com.acme.carts")] // the anchor: com.acme.carts.Cart struct Cart { customer_id: i64, items: Vec<Item>, note: Option<String>, #[serde(default)] priority: i32, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema, Schema)] #[schema(namespace = "com.acme.carts")] struct Item { sku: String, qty: u32, } The first difference fails the build with its path: error[E0080]: evaluation panicked: `Cart` does not match subject `carts-value` (migration 0001_create_cart): Cart.items[].qty: the integer type writes values outside the schema's range

cargo kafka-schema keeps every subject this service owns as numbered migrations in the repository and synchronizes them with the registry. A directory is a subject, and a migration is the full schema of one subject version. Migrations are numbered per subject, so two branches that change one subject conflict in git. subject.toml holds the format, the compatibility level, the owner, the record the subject declares, the .proto source of a Protobuf subject, and the references to other subjects. The lock records each migration's checksum and, once registered, its registry version and schema id. The lock is what the Schema derive reads offline, and a new migration rebuilds the crates that derive from it. migrate add writes the next migration from the type's own schema. It builds the crate's tests with RUSTSTREAM_SCHEMA_EXPORT set, so the derive emits no checks and a changed type exports before its migration exists. migrate run registers the pending migrations in reference order. For each, it sets the declared level, asks the registry's verbose compatibility check against every version the level names, prints the registry's messages, registers, and records the version and id in the lock. The rules: Compatibility is checked twice: locally for Avro under the subject's level, and by the registry before registering. A Protobuf field number that disappears must appear in reserved, a rule the registry does not enforce. A JSON Schema migration is validated against its draft's metaschema, and an owned JSON subject's content model must suit its level: closed at BACKWARD, open at FORWARD. Drift is an error: a registry version no migration describes, a registered migration missing from the registry, or versions in another order. The fix is migrate import or a registry cleanup. A registered migration is immutable; a change is a new migration. Migrations only go forward: a registry version cannot be undone without breaking producers. RUSTSTREAM_SCHEMA_REGISTRY names the registry, with credentials in the URL or in their own variables; the tool never prints them. Without it, every command but migrate import and migrate run works from the migrations and the lock.

prost-build generates the types from the .proto, so the type equals its source by construction. schema::build::check_proto in the build script fails the build when the compiled .proto differs from the subject's newest migration: // build.rs use ruststream_rdkafka::schema::build::check_proto; fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { prost_build::compile_protos(&["proto/payments.proto"], &["proto"])?; check_proto("payments-value")?; Ok(()) }

Commit decides what an ack or a nack does on Kafka, which settles a consumer group by committed position, not per message. A consumer group stores one offset per partition: the position its next member starts reading at. A handler settles one delivery at a time, so the subscription has to turn those outcomes into that one position. The descriptor chooses how with .commit(..): KafkaTopic, KafkaTopics and KafkaPartitions all take it. Commit::Auto is the default: librdkafka stores the position as a record is handed over and commits it on a timer. Commit::Tracked moves the position only past deliveries the handlers have settled, so a crash brings back what was not finished. Commit::Transactional hands the offsets to an exactly-once pipeline, which commits them in the producer's transaction. Under Tracked an ack and a drop both settle the offset, and nothing comes back. A retry hands the delivery back to its subscription instead.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_settlement_commit.rs /// The group's position moves past an invoice once the handler has settled it. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("invoices").group("billing").commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn book(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { if invoice.amount_cents <= 0 { // Nothing to book: a drop settles the offset like an ack, and nothing comes back. tracing::warn!(invoice.id, "invoice without an amount"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice booked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_settlement_commit.rs /// The group's position moves past an invoice once the handler has settled it. struct Book; impl Handle<Invoice, (), (), (), AppState> for Book { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if invoice.amount_cents <= 0 { // Nothing to book: a drop settles the offset like an ack, and nothing comes back. tracing::warn!(invoice.id, "invoice without an amount"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice booked"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn billing() -> KafkaTopic { KafkaTopic::new("invoices") .group("billing") .commit(Commit::Tracked) }

Commit::Auto is librdkafka's timer commit: an ack is advisory, and a retry is not delivered again. It is the default of every descriptor, and librdkafka's own default. librdkafka stores a record's position as it hands the record to the subscription, and commits the stored position every auto.commit.interval.ms. The handler's outcome changes nothing about that position: an ack and a drop are advisory. A retry reports itself unsupported, and the delivery does not come back on the subscription or on the group's next member. A crash loses the processed records whose position was not committed yet, and skips the stored records the handler had not finished. This suits a consumer that can lose a few records, such as a dashboard or a cache. A consumer that must process every record takes Commit::Tracked.

dead_letter(topic) names the topic a delivery that reached its cap is republished to, payload and headers as they arrived. It follows max_attempts(n) at the mount site. When a retry would make the delivery the n-th one, the runtime settles it and publishes it to the dead-letter topic instead. The record keeps its payload, its headers and its record key. RETRY_COUNT_HEADER on it says how many times it was delivered. A cap without a dead-letter topic rejects the spent delivery, which settles its offset, and a warning names the subscription. The dead-letter topic is the service's own infrastructure, an ordinary topic: a subscription of the same service, or of another one, reads it.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_retries.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = AppState> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| { let gateway = PaymentGateway { endpoint: "https://gateway.internal".into(), }; Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState { gateway }) }) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // Five deliveries of one payment, the first included; the fifth failure goes to // "payments.dlq" instead, payload and headers as they arrived. b.include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dlq"); b.include(on_dead_letter); }) } examples/manual/kafka_retries.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = AppState> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| { let gateway = PaymentGateway { endpoint: "https://gateway.internal".into(), }; Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState { gateway }) }) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // Five deliveries of one payment, the first included; the fifth failure goes to // "payments.dlq" instead, payload and headers as they arrived. b.include( subscriber("payments", Charge) .map_source(|_| payments()) .build(), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dlq"); b.include( subscriber("payments.dlq", OnDeadLetter) .map_source(|_| dead_letters()) .build(), ); }) } The dead-letter topic is read by an ordinary subscription: Macros Manual examples/kafka_retries.rs /// The dead-letter consumer is an ordinary subscription. The framework's retry-count header says /// how many times the payment was delivered before it was carried here. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("payments.dlq").group("payments-dlq").start(StartOffset::Earliest))] async fn on_dead_letter(payment: &Payment, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!(payment.id, deliveries, "payment dead-lettered"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_retries.rs /// The dead-letter consumer is an ordinary subscription. The framework's retry-count header says /// how many times the payment was delivered before it was carried here. struct OnDeadLetter; impl Handle<Payment, (), (), (), AppState> for OnDeadLetter { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!(payment.id, deliveries, "payment dead-lettered"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn dead_letters() -> KafkaTopic { KafkaTopic::new("payments.dlq") .group("payments-dlq") .start(StartOffset::Earliest) }

retry_after(delay) asks for a later delivery: the runtime republishes a copy to the subscription with its delivery count in a header. Kafka holds no record back and counts no deliveries, so the runtime does both. It settles the delivery, waits out the delay and publishes a copy of the record, payload and headers, to the topic the subscription reads. The copy carries RETRY_COUNT_HEADER incremented, and the handler reads it like any other header. The copy waits in the service's memory, so it is at-most-once over the delay: a process that exits before the timer fires loses it. max_attempts(n) caps the deliveries of one record at the mount site, the first one included. Under a cap every retry, an immediate one too, travels as such a copy, because the count lives in the header. The delivery that reaches the cap goes to the dead-letter topic. The copies leave through the Retry slot, which out_retry replaces. A subscription over several topics names where its copies go, as ToSourceTopic shows.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_retries.rs /// A transient failure asks for a later delivery. Kafka cannot hold a record back, so the /// runtime waits out the delay and publishes a copy to the topic this subscription reads, with /// the retry-count header incremented. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("payments").group("payments-svc").commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn charge(payment: &Payment, State(gateway): State<PaymentGateway>) -> HandlerOutcome { if payment.amount_cents <= 0 { // Malformed input is not worth retrying: dropping it settles the offset. return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } match gateway.charge(payment).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "charge failed, retrying"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } } } examples/manual/kafka_retries.rs /// A transient failure asks for a later delivery. Kafka cannot hold a record back, so the /// runtime waits out the delay and publishes a copy to the topic this subscription reads, with /// the retry-count header incremented. struct Charge; impl Handle<Payment, (), (), (), AppState> for Charge { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if payment.amount_cents <= 0 { // Malformed input is not worth retrying: dropping it settles the offset. return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } if let Err(err) = ctx.state().gateway.charge(payment).await { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "charge failed, retrying"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK)); } Ok(()) } } fn payments() -> KafkaTopic { KafkaTopic::new("payments") .group("payments-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) }

ToSourceTopic sends each retry copy back to the topic its delivery arrived on, for subscriptions over several topics. A KafkaTopic subscription reads one topic, and its retry copies go there. A KafkaTopics list or pattern and a KafkaPartitions reader have no single topic, so the mount site names one. ToSourceTopic is a transform of the Retry slot: .out_retry(Publish::default()).transform(ToSourceTopic). It reads each delivery's topic from its Kafka context, so a copy of an orders-us record goes back to orders-us. The context reaches the slot when the handler reads it: a Ctx<Topic> parameter, or a manual body typed over KafkaContext. A batch handler carries no per-record topic, so a batch registration names a fixed topic instead. .out_retry(Publish::default()).to(topic) sends every copy to that one topic; a pattern that matches it reads the copies back. A registration over several topics that names neither does not start.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_settlement_source_topic.rs /// One subscription reads both regions. Reading the topic is also what hands the Kafka context /// to the retry position, where `ToSourceTopic` reads it. #[subscriber(KafkaTopics::new(["orders-eu", "orders-us"]).group("orders-svc").commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn reserve( order: &Order, Ctx(topic): Ctx<Topic>, State(warehouse): State<Arc<Warehouse>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { if let Err(err) = warehouse.reserve(order) { tracing::warn!(order.id, %topic, err, "warehouse unavailable, retrying"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, %topic, "stock reserved"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_settlement_source_topic.rs /// One subscription reads both regions. A body typed over `KafkaContext` hands that context to /// the retry position, where `ToSourceTopic` reads it. struct Reserve; impl Handle<Order, (), (), KafkaContext, AppState> for Reserve { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext, AppState>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let topic = ctx.context(Topic); if let Err(err) = ctx.state().warehouse.reserve(order) { tracing::warn!(order.id, %topic, err, "warehouse unavailable, retrying"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } tracing::info!(order.id, %topic, "stock reserved"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn regions() -> KafkaTopics { KafkaTopics::new(["orders-eu", "orders-us"]) .group("orders-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) } Macros Manual examples/kafka_settlement_source_topic.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = AppState> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState::default())) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // A copy goes back to the topic its delivery arrived on. b.include(reserve) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("dlq.orders") .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToSourceTopic); // Every copy goes to one topic. `.to(topic)` belongs to the publisher the copies // leave through, so it follows `out_retry`. b.include(post_entry) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("dlq.ledger") .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("ledger.retry"); }) } examples/manual/kafka_settlement_source_topic.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = AppState> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState::default())) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // A copy goes back to the topic its delivery arrived on. b.include( subscriber("orders-eu,orders-us", Reserve) .map_source(|_| regions()) .build(), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("dlq.orders") .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToSourceTopic); Macros Manual examples/kafka_settlement_source_topic.rs /// A pattern reads every ledger topic there is; its copies go to one retry topic the pattern /// also matches, so they come back to this subscription. #[subscriber(KafkaTopicPattern::new("^ledger\\..*").group("ledger-svc").commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn post_entry(entry: &Entry, State(ledger): State<Arc<Ledger>>) -> HandlerOutcome { if let Err(err) = ledger.post(entry) { tracing::warn!(entry.order_id, err, "ledger unavailable, retrying"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_settlement_source_topic.rs /// A pattern reads every ledger topic there is; its copies go to one retry topic the pattern /// also matches, so they come back to this subscription. struct PostEntry; impl Handle<Entry, (), (), (), AppState> for PostEntry { fn handle( &self, entry: &Entry, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if let Err(err) = ctx.state().ledger.post(entry) { tracing::warn!(entry.order_id, err, "ledger unavailable, retrying"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } ready(Ok(())) } } fn ledgers() -> KafkaTopicPattern { KafkaTopics::pattern("^ledger\\..*") .group("ledger-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) }

Commit::Tracked commits below the lowest unsettled delivery, so a retry comes back and nothing is committed past it. The subscription stores a position only when a handler settles a delivery. The stored position is the offset just below the lowest delivery still in flight, so handlers that finish out of order, on several workers, never commit past an unfinished one. librdkafka's timer commits the stored position in the background and once more when the consumer closes. An ack and a drop settle the offset. A retry hands the delivery back to its subscription, which delivers it again before the records behind it. Until it is settled, the group's committed position stays below it, so a crash or a rebalance brings it to the next member. Offsets the consumer never receives, such as transaction markers and compacted records, do not hold the position back. Tracked with an idempotent producer gives at-least-once from input to output, as Durability shows.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_settlement_commit.rs /// A charge the gateway turned away comes back on this subscription before anything behind it, /// and the group commits nothing past it until it is settled. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("charges").group("payments").commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn take_charge(charge: &Charge, State(gateway): State<Arc<Gateway>>) -> HandlerOutcome { if let Err(err) = gateway.charge(charge) { tracing::warn!(%err, "charge retried"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(charge.id, "charge taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_settlement_commit.rs /// A charge the gateway turned away comes back on this subscription before anything behind it, /// and the group commits nothing past it until it is settled. struct TakeCharge; impl Handle<Charge, (), (), (), AppState> for TakeCharge { fn handle( &self, charge: &Charge, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if let Err(err) = ctx.state().gateway.charge(charge) { tracing::warn!(%err, "charge retried"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } tracing::info!(charge.id, "charge taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn payments() -> KafkaTopic { KafkaTopic::new("charges") .group("payments") .commit(Commit::Tracked) }

A topic name in #[subscriber] reads that topic in the broker's default group; a descriptor carries every other setting. #[subscriber("orders")] reads the topic orders. Kafka reads a topic only through a consumer group, and a bare name names none, so the group comes from KafkaBroker::default_group. A subscription with no group, on a broker with no default group, stops the service at startup with an error that names the subscription. Two subscriptions of one name and one group are two members of that group: each record goes to one of them. Every other setting of a subscription belongs to a descriptor: KafkaTopic for one topic, KafkaTopics for several topics, KafkaTopicPattern for every topic a regex matches, and KafkaPartitions for named partitions. A descriptor goes where the name goes, as the attribute's first argument. The manual form passes the name to subscriber(name, body), and a descriptor joins the chain through map_source. A subscription is open once its group has assigned it its partitions, so everything published after startup reaches it. Startup waits for that assignment up to KafkaBroker::assignment_timeout, 60 seconds by default.

The topic orders, read in the group orders-svc. Macros Manual examples/kafka_subscriptions_name.rs /// Reads the topic `orders`; the group comes from the broker. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders-svc"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(place); }) } examples/manual/kafka_subscriptions_name.rs /// Reads the topic `orders`; the group comes from the broker. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders-svc"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()); }) }

Assignment picks the consumer group's rebalance strategy, eager or cooperative sticky. A group hands each partition of its topics to one member, and hands them out again when a member joins or leaves. The setting is librdkafka's partition.assignment.strategy, written on the descriptor with assignment. Assignment::Range and Assignment::RoundRobin are eager: every member gives up all its partitions at each rebalance, and the group stops reading until the new assignment lands. Assignment::CooperativeSticky is incremental: only the partitions that change hands move, and the rest keep flowing during the rebalance. Without the setting librdkafka uses range,roundrobin. Every member of one group must use the same family: librdkafka refuses a cooperative member in an eager group, and the error surfaces on the subscription. KafkaPartitions joins no group and has no assignment.

A cooperative sticky group reads every shipment once, whichever member holds its partition. Macros Manual examples/kafka_subscriptions_assignment.rs /// Ships each shipment; a rebalance moves only the partitions that change hands. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("warehouse.shipments") .start(StartOffset::Earliest) .assignment(Assignment::CooperativeSticky) )] async fn ship(shipment: &Shipment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(shipment.id, "shipped"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_subscriptions_assignment.rs /// Ships each shipment it reads. struct Ship; impl Handle<Shipment> for Ship { fn handle( &self, shipment: &Shipment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(shipment.id, "shipped"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(servers: &str, group: &str) -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new([servers]).default_group(group); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("warehouse", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // A rebalance moves only the partitions that change hands. let shipments = KafkaTopic::new("warehouse.shipments") .start(StartOffset::Earliest) .assignment(Assignment::CooperativeSticky); b.include( subscriber("warehouse.shipments", Ship) .build() .map_source(|_| shipments), ); }) }

A slice handler reads one fetched delivery plus what librdkafka already holds, up to the size the mount site names. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. The size travels down to the consumer's poll, which never hands the body more than n records. librdkafka fetches records ahead in the background, and a batch takes what it already holds without waiting for more. So a batch is often smaller than n, and a quiet topic yields batches of one. One outcome settles every record of the batch. A Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles record i with outcome i. Under Commit::Tracked a record that asks to come back holds the committed position in front of it until it settles; a process that stops first replays the acked records behind it too. A retry_after in a batch becomes a copy published back to the topic after the delay, so the registration names its retry publisher with .out_retry(policy). How much librdkafka queues locally is a consumer property, set through the descriptor's passthrough (queued.max.messages.kbytes, fetch.queue.backoff.ms). workers(n) keeps up to n batches in flight at once. A batch body reads a KafkaBatchContext, which carries the seek handle and no per-record field. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) acks the batch and Err(outcomes) settles record by record.

Three orders waiting in the consumer's queue arrive in one call. Macros Manual examples/kafka_batches.rs /// Stores a batch of orders in one round-trip; one outcome settles the whole batch. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("orders").group("orders-svc").commit(Commit::Tracked), workers(4) )] async fn store(orders: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "stored in one round-trip"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // At most 64 orders per call. b.include(store.batch(nonzero!(64))); }) } examples/manual/kafka_batches.rs /// Stores a batch of orders in one round-trip; `Ok` settles the whole batch. struct Store; impl Handle<[Order]> for Store { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "stored in one round-trip"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = KafkaTopic::new("orders") .group("orders-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked); // At most 64 orders per call, up to four calls at once. b.include( subscriber("orders", Store) .batch(nonzero!(64)) .workers(nonzero!(4)) .build() .map_source(|_| orders), ); }) }

Only the unsettled payment comes back, as a copy published after the delay. Macros Manual examples/kafka_batches.rs /// One outcome per payment, in slice order: only the unsettled ones come back. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("payments") .group("payments-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) .config("queued.max.messages.kbytes", "1024") )] async fn reconcile(payments: &[Payment]) -> Vec<HandlerOutcome> { payments .iter() .map(|payment| { if payment.settled { HandlerOutcome::ack() } else { HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } }) .collect() } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // A delayed retry is a copy published back to the topic after the delay. b.include(reconcile.batch(nonzero!(16))) .out_retry(Publish::default()); }) } examples/manual/kafka_batches.rs /// One outcome per payment, in slice order: only the unsettled ones come back. struct Reconcile; impl Handle<[Payment]> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, payments: &[Payment], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { ready(Err(payments .iter() .map(|payment| { if payment.settled { HandlerOutcome::ack() } else { HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } }) .collect())) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let payments = KafkaTopic::new("payments") .group("payments-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) .config("queued.max.messages.kbytes", "1024"); // A delayed retry is a copy published back to the topic after the delay. b.include( subscriber("payments", Reconcile) .batch(nonzero!(16)) .build() .map_source(|_| payments), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()); }) }

KafkaPartitions reads exactly the partitions it names, joins no group and never rebalances. KafkaPartitions::new takes the topic and its partition numbers. It suits a reader pinned to a partition, an inspection or replay tool, and one consumer per partition. The reader takes no part in the group protocol, so group members on the same topic neither see it nor take its partitions away. A group stays optional and decides only where offsets go. With group the reader commits into that group without joining it. Without a group it commits nothing, so start must name Earliest or Latest: Committed has nothing to resume from and stops the service at startup. commit, lane_key and config work as on KafkaTopic; Commit::Transactional stops the service at startup, because an exactly-once pipeline commits through the group protocol. Under the default lane key each named partition gets a lane of its own. The subscription's name is the topic. No publish addresses a subset of partitions, so a registration names where a retry copy goes, as the example does with .out_retry(policy).to("orders.retry").

Partition 0 of orders, read from its first record by a service that names no group. Macros Manual examples/kafka_subscriptions_partitions.rs /// Inspects partition 0 of `orders` from its first record, with no group of its own. #[subscriber(KafkaPartitions::new("orders", [0]).start(StartOffset::Earliest))] async fn inspect(order: &Order, Ctx(offset): Ctx<Offset>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, offset, "partition 0"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { // The broker names no group, and the reader needs none. let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("inspector", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // No publish reaches exactly these partitions, so a retried order goes to a topic of // its own. b.include(inspect) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("orders.retry"); }) } examples/manual/kafka_subscriptions_partitions.rs /// Logs each order with its offset in the partition. struct Inspect; impl Handle<Order, (), (), KafkaContext> for Inspect { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, offset = ctx.context(Offset), "partition 0"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // The broker names no group, and the reader needs none. let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("inspector", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Partition 0 of `orders`, from its first record. let partition = KafkaPartitions::new("orders", [0]).start(StartOffset::Earliest); // No publish reaches exactly these partitions, so a retried order goes to a topic of // its own. b.include( subscriber("orders", Inspect) .build() .map_source(|_| partition), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("orders.retry"); }) }

KafkaTopic reads one topic in one consumer group, with its start offset, commit mode, assignment and lane key. KafkaTopic::new takes the topic, and every other setting is optional. An unset setting keeps librdkafka's own default; the crate adds none of its own. group names the consumer group and overrides the broker's default_group. start is the start offset of a group that has committed nothing yet. commit is the commit mode, which decides what an ack does. assignment is the group's rebalance strategy, and lane_key is what keyed lanes are keyed by. config passes any other consumer property to librdkafka. The subscription's name is the topic: a test reads its deliveries under that name, and the AsyncAPI document reports that channel. A publish to the topic reaches every group that reads it, so a delayed retry copy goes back to the topic with no setting at the mount site. A topic name that Kafka refuses, or a name that starts with ^, stops the service at startup; a pattern is KafkaTopicPattern. schema turns on schema checking for the topic.

Every order of orders is confirmed by the group orders-workers, and the confirmation goes to the topic its type declares. Macros Manual examples/kafka_topics.rs /// Confirms every order of the topic `orders`, as a member of the group `orders-workers`. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("orders") .group("orders-workers") .start(StartOffset::Earliest) .commit(Commit::Tracked) .assignment(Assignment::CooperativeSticky) .config("fetch.min.bytes", "1024"), reply )] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id, accepted: true, } } examples/manual/kafka_topics.rs /// Confirms every order it reads. struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id, accepted: true, })) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // The topic `orders`, read as a member of the group `orders-workers`. let orders = KafkaTopic::new("orders") .group("orders-workers") .start(StartOffset::Earliest) .commit(Commit::Tracked) .assignment(Assignment::CooperativeSticky) .config("fetch.min.bytes", "1024"); b.include( subscriber("orders", Confirm) .reply() .build() .map_source(|_| orders), ); }) }

KafkaTopics reads a list of topics through one consumer and one group, and each delivery names its topic. KafkaTopics::new takes the topics, and and_topic adds one more. The group settings are the ones KafkaTopic has: group, start, commit, assignment, lane_key and config. Every topic of the list shares the handler, so every topic carries the handler's payload type. Ctx<Topic> binds the topic a delivery came from. The subscription's name is the list joined with commas, orders,cancellations here. No one publish reaches a list again, so a registration over it names where a retry copy goes: .out_retry(policy).to(topic), or ToSourceTopic to send each copy back to the topic it came from. A registration that names neither stops the service at startup. schema(topic, namespace) turns on schema checking for one topic of the list, addressed by its name. Every topic a regex matches is a pattern, a descriptor of its own.

Order events from two topics become one history, and each entry names the topic of its event. Macros Manual examples/kafka_multi_topic.rs /// Reads two topics through one consumer of the group `order-history`. #[subscriber( KafkaTopics::new(["orders", "cancellations"]).group("order-history"), reply )] async fn record(event: &OrderEvent, Ctx(topic): Ctx<Topic>) -> HistoryEntry { HistoryEntry { id: event.id, topic: topic.to_string(), } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // No one topic reaches a topic set again, so the mount site says where a retried // event goes: back to the topic it came from. b.include(record) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToSourceTopic); }) } examples/manual/kafka_multi_topic.rs /// Answers each event with a history entry naming the topic it came from. struct Record; impl Handle<OrderEvent, HistoryEntry, (), KafkaContext> for Record { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderEvent, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<HistoryEntry, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(HistoryEntry { id: event.id, topic: ctx.context(Topic).to_string(), })) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Two topics through one consumer of the group `order-history`. let events = KafkaTopics::new(["orders", "cancellations"]).group("order-history"); // No one topic reaches a topic set again, so the mount site says where a retried // event goes: back to the topic it came from. b.include( subscriber("orders,cancellations", Record) .reply() .build() .map_source(|_| events), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToSourceTopic); }) }

LaneKey decides what workers(n, by_key) keys a lane by: the source partition, or the record key. workers(n, by_key) runs n sequential lanes: deliveries with one lane key run in order on one lane, and different keys run at once. On Kafka the descriptor's lane_key decides what that key is. LaneKey::Partition, the default, keys a lane by the partition the record came from, Kafka's own unit of order. Everything one partition delivers then runs in order, keyless records included, and partitions run side by side. LaneKey::RecordKey keys a lane by the record's native key, which is finer than a partition. One key's records stay in order, and records of different keys run at once even inside one partition. A keyless record has no lane key under RecordKey; it rotates over the lanes and loses its partition order. The publish side sets the record key from the partition-key header, so a record published with a key reaches its lane by that key. The manual form writes the lanes as .workers_by_key(n) on the mount chain.

Two tenants' orders, each order a second of work: lanes by record key run the tenants side by side, two seconds in all. Macros Manual examples/kafka_keys.rs /// Eight lanes by record key: one tenant's orders run in order, different tenants at once, /// even inside one partition. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("orders").group("orders-workers").lane_key(LaneKey::RecordKey), workers(8, by_key) )] async fn on_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { process(order).await; HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_keys.rs /// Eight lanes by record key: one tenant's orders run in order, different tenants at once, /// even inside one partition. fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = KafkaTopic::new("orders") .group("orders-workers") .lane_key(LaneKey::RecordKey); b.include( subscriber("orders", Process) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(8)) .build() .map_source(|_| orders), ); }) }

The same four orders on a topic with one partition take four seconds: the partition is one lane. Macros Manual examples/kafka_keys.rs /// Eight lanes by source partition, the default: everything one partition delivers runs in /// order on one lane, keyless records included. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("audit").group("audit-workers"), workers(8, by_key))] async fn on_audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { process(order).await; HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_keys.rs /// Eight lanes by source partition, the default: everything one partition delivers runs in /// order on one lane, keyless records included. fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let audit = KafkaTopic::new("audit").group("audit-workers"); b.include( subscriber("audit", Process) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(8)) .build() .map_source(|_| audit), ); }) }

A descriptor's config passes any consumer property; one the commit mode owns is refused at startup, naming the property. KafkaTopic::config, and the same method on KafkaTopics and KafkaPartitions, sets one librdkafka consumer property by its name. It reaches the properties the descriptor has no typed option for: fetch sizes, queue limits, timeouts. The passthrough applies last, so it wins over the typed options and over the broker-wide configuration. A property the commit mode owns is the exception. Under Commit::Tracked and Commit::Transactional the crate computes the committed position itself, through enable.auto.offset.store and enable.auto.commit. A passthrough that sets either one would leave the position to librdkafka while every ack decided nothing. So the subscription refuses to open, and the startup error names the subscription and the property. Commit::Auto owns neither property and takes both from the passthrough. A property for every consumer of the broker goes on KafkaBroker instead.

fetch.queue.backoff.ms shortens the pause librdkafka takes when a partition's local queue is full, from a second to 10 ms. Macros Manual examples/kafka_subscriptions_passthrough.rs /// Settles payments; librdkafka pauses a full partition for 10 ms instead of a second. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("payments") .group("payments-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) .config("fetch.queue.backoff.ms", "10") )] async fn settle(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(payment.id, "settled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_subscriptions_passthrough.rs /// Settles every payment it reads. struct Settle; impl Handle<Payment> for Settle { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(payment.id, "settled"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // librdkafka pauses a full partition for 10 ms instead of a second. let payments = KafkaTopic::new("payments") .group("payments-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) .config("fetch.queue.backoff.ms", "10"); b.include( subscriber("payments", Settle) .build() .map_source(|_| payments), ); }) }

KafkaTopicPattern reads every topic a librdkafka regex starting with ^ matches, those created later included. The leading ^ is how librdkafka tells a pattern from a topic name. A pattern without it stops the service at startup, because librdkafka would subscribe to it as a literal name. KafkaTopicPattern::new takes the pattern, and and_pattern adds another one to the same subscription. KafkaTopics::pattern builds the same descriptor; the #[subscriber] attribute takes the type its constructor names, so the attribute starts from KafkaTopicPattern::new. The group settings are the ones KafkaTopic has. The consumer finds a topic created after startup on its next metadata refresh, and the group then assigns its partitions. A new topic is read from where the start offset puts it. The subscription's name is the pattern itself. A delivery names the topic it came from through Ctx<Topic>, and a retry copy needs a destination named at the mount site, as on KafkaTopics. Sets of the matched topics opt into schema checking with .schema(pattern, namespace).

Every topic under audit. is archived; auditing is not. Macros Manual examples/kafka_multi_topic.rs /// Reads every topic whose name starts with `audit.`, those created later included. #[subscriber(KafkaTopicPattern::new("^audit\\..*").group("audit-archive"))] async fn archive(event: &OrderEvent, Ctx(topic): Ctx<Topic>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(event.id, %topic, "archived"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // A retried event goes back to the topic it came from. b.include(archive) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToSourceTopic); }) } examples/manual/kafka_multi_topic.rs /// Archives an event, logging the topic it came from. struct Archive; impl Handle<OrderEvent, (), (), KafkaContext> for Archive { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderEvent, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(event.id, topic = %ctx.context(Topic), "archived"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Every topic whose name starts with `audit.`, those created later included. let audit = KafkaTopics::pattern("^audit\\..*").group("audit-archive"); // A retried event goes back to the topic it came from. b.include( subscriber("^audit\\..*", Archive) .build() .map_source(|_| audit), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToSourceTopic); }) }

schema(namespace) on a descriptor checks at startup that the topic's registry subjects exist and declare records of that namespace. A topic opts in one by one; a topic without schema is checked against no registry and costs nothing. The namespace is the one its records carry: com.acme.orders for com.acme.orders.Order. The subjects follow TopicNameStrategy: orders-value for the payload of orders, orders-key for its key. Schema::namespace names other subjects with .value(..) and .key(..); a plain string is the namespace with the default subjects. The check reads the registry of KafkaBroker::schema_prefetch, once per topic, while the subscription opens. A broker with no registry stops the service at startup when a topic opts in. What stops the service, with the topic, the subject, where its name came from, and the fix in the error: the value subject is missing from the registry; the newest schema of the value subject declares no record of the namespace; a key subject named with .key(..) is missing; a key subject that exists declares records, none of them of the namespace. A key subject the topic's name gives may be missing: a topic with plain string keys registers none. An Avro subject declares its record, or each record of a union; a Protobuf subject declares its top-level messages in its package. A JSON Schema names no record, so a JSON subject is checked for presence only. Each form opts in with the arguments it needs: KafkaTopic::schema(namespace) for its one topic; KafkaTopics::schema(topic, namespace) for one topic of the list, addressed by name; a name the list does not hold stops the service and names the list; KafkaTopicPattern::schema(pattern, namespace) for a set of the matched topics. The sets of a pattern narrow in the order they are written: a topic takes the first set whose pattern it matches. Each topic of a set has its own default subjects (orders.eu-value), and an override names one subject for the whole set. A matched topic that no set takes is not checked. The topics the cluster holds when the subscription opens are checked at startup. A topic created later is checked when the group first assigns it to the member, and a mismatch then is logged.

orders is checked against orders-value; of the two listed topics, returns names its own value subject. Macros Manual examples/kafka_subscriptions_schema.rs /// `orders` is checked against `orders-value`, the subject its name gives. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("orders").schema("com.acme.orders"))] async fn on_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Each listed topic opts in by name; `returns` names its value subject. #[subscriber( KafkaTopics::new(["refunds", "returns"]) .schema("refunds", "com.acme.orders") .schema("returns", Schema::namespace("com.acme.orders").value("returns-v2")) )] async fn on_settlement(order: &Order, Ctx(topic): Ctx<Topic>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, %topic, "settled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app(registry: &str) -> impl App { let prefetch = SchemaPrefetch::new(SchemaRegistry::new(registry)); let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]) .default_group("orders-svc") .schema_prefetch(prefetch); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(on_order); b.include(on_settlement) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("settlements.retry"); }) } examples/manual/kafka_subscriptions_schema.rs /// Places an order. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(registry: &str) -> impl App { let prefetch = SchemaPrefetch::new(SchemaRegistry::new(registry)); let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]) .default_group("orders-svc") .schema_prefetch(prefetch); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // `orders` is checked against `orders-value`, the subject its name gives. let orders = KafkaTopic::new("orders").schema("com.acme.orders"); b.include(subscriber(orders, Place).build()); // Each listed topic opts in by name; `returns` names its value subject. let settlements = KafkaTopics::new(["refunds", "returns"]) .schema("refunds", "com.acme.orders") .schema( "returns", Schema::namespace("com.acme.orders").value("returns-v2"), );
